pages.text: Imagine one speck of gold dust from Obuasi on the tip of a pin. Cut it in half, then in half again, and keep going. Could you go on for ever? About 2,400 years ago, a Greek thinker named Democritus said no. He believed you would finally reach a piece too small to be cut, and he called it an atom. He had no way to test the idea. Today we know that atoms are real. That one speck of gold contains more atoms than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of Ghana.

He had no way to test the idea.

That one speck of gold contains more atoms than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of Ghana.

pages.text: An atom is not a solid ball. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford showed that it is mostly empty space. At the centre is a tiny, heavy nucleus, made of particles called protons and neutrons. Protons have a positive charge, and neutrons have none. Far outside the nucleus move the electrons, which are very light and negatively charged. If an atom were the size of the Baba Yara Stadium in Kumasi, the nucleus would be a small bead on the centre spot. Yet almost all of the mass of the atom is packed into that bead.
sentences: An atom is not a solid ball.
In 1911, Ernest Rutherford showed that it is mostly empty space.
At the centre is a tiny, heavy nucleus, made of particles called protons and neutrons.
Protons have a positive charge, and neutrons have none.
Far outside the nucleus move the electrons, which are very light and negatively charged.
If an atom were the size of the Baba Yara Stadium in Kumasi, the nucleus would be a small bead on the centre spot.
Yet almost all of the mass of the atom is packed into that bead.
pages.alt: A simple drawing of an atom with a small central nucleus of red and blue particles and electrons moving far around it.

pages.text: In 1938, in Germany, Otto Hahn fired neutrons at uranium, the heaviest atom found in nature, and was puzzled to find a much lighter element among the products. He wrote to Lise Meitner, a physicist who had worked beside him for thirty years. She was Jewish and had fled from Germany to Sweden to escape the Nazis. Meitner worked out what had happened. The uranium nucleus had split in two, releasing a great deal of energy. The process was named nuclear fission. Hahn alone received a Nobel Prize for it. Many scientists think Meitner should have shared it.

He wrote to Lise Meitner, a physicist who had worked beside him for thirty years.
She was Jewish and had fled from Germany to Sweden to escape the Nazis.
Meitner worked out what had happened.
The uranium nucleus had split in two, releasing a great deal of energy.
The process was named nuclear fission.
Hahn alone received a Nobel Prize for it.
Many scientists think Meitner should have shared it.
pages.alt: A large nucleus being struck by a small particle and splitting into two smaller pieces with a burst of light.

pages.text: Each uranium nucleus that splits also throws out two or three neutrons. If these strike other nuclei, those split as well, and release more neutrons, and so on. This is a chain reaction. Controlled carefully, it gives steady heat. Let loose, it gives an explosion. The Second World War had begun, and scientists feared that Germany would build such a bomb first. The United States gathered thousands of scientists in a secret project to build one. Meitner was invited to join. She refused, saying she would have nothing to do with a bomb.

She refused, saying she would have nothing to do with a bomb.
pages.alt: One splitting nucleus sending out particles that split two more, which split four more, spreading like branches.

pages.text: In August 1945, American aircraft dropped atomic bombs on two Japanese cities, Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Well over 100,000 people died, most of them ordinary families, and many survivors suffered for the rest of their lives. The war ended days later, but the world had changed. Other countries built their own bombs. By 1986 there were about 70,000 nuclear warheads. Treaties have since reduced the number: in January 2026 nine countries held about 12,200 between them. That is far fewer, but still enough to destroy civilisation, and the fall in numbers has almost stopped.

pages.text: The same knowledge also serves life. Controlled fission produces electricity in power stations, and materials made in reactors are used to find and treat cancer. Africa has made a clear choice. Under a treaty that came into force in 2009, the whole continent is a zone free of nuclear weapons, and Ghana is a member. Kwame Nkrumah set up the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission at Kwabenya in 1963 to use the atom for health, farming, and energy. Knowledge itself is neither good nor bad. What matters is what people decide to do with it. Soon, some of those decisions will be yours.

activities.question: Where is most of the mass of an atom found?
What is nuclear fission?
options: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller ones, releasing energy
The joining of two atoms to make gold
The movement of electrons round a circuit

activities.question: What keeps a chain reaction going?
options: Neutrons released by each splitting nucleus go on to split others

activities.question: Apply it: A classmate says, “Nuclear science is evil and should never have been discovered.” Which reply is best supported by the article?
options: Agree, because it has only ever been used for bombs
It also serves power and medicine; what matters is how people choose to use it
Disagree, because the bombs harmed nobody

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Democritus suggests that matter is made of atoms
Rutherford shows that the atom has a tiny nucleus
Hahn and Meitner discover nuclear fission
Atomic bombs are dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Africa becomes a zone free of nuclear weapons

glossary.definition: The smallest particle of an element.
The tiny, heavy centre of an atom.
Positively charged particles in the nucleus.
Particles in the nucleus that have no charge.
Very light, negatively charged particles that move around the nucleus.
Nuclear fission: the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller ones, releasing energy.
Chain reaction: a process in which each splitting nucleus causes more nuclei to split.
